contexts.story: Open by reframing career growth in the AI era: the landscape is shifting fast, and the real risk is standing still, not moving. Set the tone that this talk is a practical guide to growing with the industry, not fighting it.

Show how AI work has changed from traditional, linear model-building to LLM-centric orchestration, to explain why old career playbooks are no longer enough. This sets the context for why we must update our growth strategies.

Translate the industry shift into concrete role changes: what engineers and applied scientists are now expected to do, and where the highest-value work is moving. This helps the audience see how their day-to-day work will evolve.

Introduce a three-part framework for personal career leverage in the LLM era—problem definition, evaluation/tuning, and cross-domain combination—so the audience has a simple mental model for where to invest effort.
Deep-dive into how to define high-value problems and design robust systems using practical processes, showing that good framing and architecture are now core career skills, not nice-to-haves.

Cover practical, repeatable techniques for working with LLMs—prompt tuning, understanding its limits, and preventing error cascades—so people can turn AI from a toy into a reliable partner in their work.

Highlight enduring human advantages—system-level thinking and low-level performance skills—and use a brief anecdote to show how local optimization without system awareness can hurt both products and careers.
Zoom out to long-term career strategy: roles will consolidate and change (like manual testers did), so the winning move is to keep evolving your skill set and identity along with the industry.
Offer a concrete, time-efficient routine for staying current with AI and turning learning into reusable workflows, including using LLMs as a "single source of truth" translator for your work.
Close with a simple, memorable principle—"make every step solid"—tying together mindset and execution so the audience leaves with a clear daily practice for compounding career growth.
